title: High Income Countries Approach Universal Women’s Bank Account Ownership; but Progress for Lower Income Countries Remains Slow
text: Faceted density plot of the share of women who own a bank account, by country income group, for 2011, 2017, 2021 and 2024.

title: High Income Countries Approach Universal Women’s Bank Account Ownership; but Progress for Lower Income Countries Remains Slow
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization looks at how the share of women with bank accounts has shifted across countries at different income levels, from 2011 to 2024, using data from the World Bank’s Global Findex Database. The audience again are policy stakeholders and development researchers. The purpose is to show that progress on women’s financial access has not been evenly distributed. High income countries show a sharp rightward shift in their distribution after 2021, likely due to payment digitization during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite the expansion of mobile money in Sub-Saharan Africa from around 2014, low income countries show little movement in the share of women who own bank accounts across the 4 survey years.

title: High Income Countries Approach Universal Women’s Bank Account Ownership; but Progress for Lower Income Countries Remains Slow
text:
Sources

Global Findex Database (World Bank)

title: Economic performance is a poor proxy for mental wellbeing across world regions (2000-2022)
text: Two heatmaps by income group, 2000-2022: GDP per capita growth rate (top) and suicide mortality rate per 100,000 (bottom).

title: Economic performance is a poor proxy for mental wellbeing across world regions (2000-2022)
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization is intended for policymakers and mental health researchers, and is designed to be accessible with limited prior technical knowledge if any. The two heatmaps intend to show the disconnect between economic performance and mental health outcomes across income groups from 2000 to 2022. GDP per capita growth rates fluctuate sharply, with notable contractions in 2008 (due to the financial crisis) and 2020 (due to the COVID-19 pandemic). At the same time, suicide mortality rates remain more or less the same or decline only gradually over the same period. High income countries, despite steady economic recovery after 2010, record some of the highest suicide mortality rates globally.

title: Economic performance is a poor proxy for mental wellbeing across world regions (2000-2022)
text:
Sources

World Bank open database: NY.GDP.PCAP.KD.ZG
World Bank open database: SH.STA.SUIC.P5

title: Global credit access has grown unevenly across income groups (1990-2024)
text: Line chart of domestic private sector credit as a % of GDP, 1990-2024, for high, upper middle, lower middle and low income countries and China.

title: Global credit access has grown unevenly across income groups (1990-2024)
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization is intended for policymakers, economists and the general public, and is meant to be accessible without prior technical knowledge. The line chart tracks domestic credit to the private sector as a percentage of GDP across four World Bank income groups and China from 1990 to 2024. While high income countries have maintained consistently high credit levels throughout the period, the most striking trend is China’s rapid expansion since 2008, which has seen it surpass high income averages and approach 200% of GDP by 2024, thus also driving the remarkable growth we see in the upper middle income credit levels.
At the same time, low income countries have roughly under 15% throughout with hardly any increase.

title: Global credit access has grown unevenly across income groups (1990-2024)
text:
Sources

World Bank open database: FS.AST.PRVT.GD.ZS

title: Antenatal Care Coverage in Rural and Urban Bangladesh over the Decades
text: Faceted line chart of antenatal care coverage among pregnant women in Bangladesh, rural versus urban, for no visits, one visit and four or more visits (WHO recommended).

title: Antenatal Care Coverage in Rural and Urban Bangladesh over the Decades
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization is intended for public health policymakers, maternal health advocates, and the general public. It is designed to be interpreted even without deep statistical expertise. The faceted line chart tracks antenatal care (ANC) coverage among pregnant women in Bangladesh from the mid-1990s to the early 2020s, disaggregated by rural and urban residence across three levels of care:

no visits,
one visit, and
four or more visits. (this being the WHO-recommended standard).

What we see is a persistent and meaningful urban-rural gap. Rural women have historically been far more likely to receive no antenatal care at all, while urban women are consistently more likely to achieve the WHO-recommended threshold of four or more visits. Although both groups show improvement over time, the gap has not closed. By the early 2020s, rural women still fall behind urban women on adequate care coverage by roughly 20 percentage points.

title: Antenatal Care Coverage in Rural and Urban Bangladesh over the Decades
text:
Sources

data.unicef.org/topic/maternal-health/antenatal-care

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
text:
Download the full data story (PDF)
When it comes to healthcare, the right infrastructure can mean the difference between life and death. But what happens when the infrastructure exists on paper but millions still go without care? Data collected through Round 9 of the Afrobarometer survey (2021-23) reveals a sharp disconnect across 39 countries in Africa. Bad roads can make the journey to accessing health facilities arduous, but the story doesn’t necessarily end there. For those who make it to a clinic, their experience there might matter just as much, if not more. Of the many factors that affect health-seeking behaviour, this story examines two possible explanations for low uptake of healthcare services in countries on the African continent.

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
section: Proximity to a clinic doesn’t guarantee access to medicines or medical treatment
text:
Proximity to a clinic doesn’t guarantee access to medicines or medical treatment
Data shows that having a health clinic within walking distance does not automatically translate to access to medical care. In Cameroon, for instance, over 85% of communities had a clinic nearby, however, nearly 75% of households still reported going without medicines or medical treatment in the past 12 months. In contrast, Mauritius, one of Africa’s higher-income countries, shows nearly equal shares of clinic access and care received. It offers a glimpse of what the relationship between proximity and care could look like.



Dumbbell chart comparing, for 15 African countries, the share of communities with a clinic nearby and the share of households that received care. Cameroon, Senegal and Tunisia have the highest clinic access; Mauritius shows nearly equal shares.


Perhaps more relevant to understanding why people go without care is to ask: what happens once you do get to the clinic?

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
section: Patient experiences highlight troubling realities in public clinics
text:
Patient experiences highlight troubling realities in public clinics
Responses regarding experiences with the healthcare system provide some striking insight into the various challenges patients encounter. Of those who sought care at a public clinic, 1 in 2 in Liberia and Sierra Leone paid a bribe to healthcare workers in order to access care. A shockingly large share also reported medicines being unavailable and facing long wait times. The lack of respect also emerged as a theme in some countries. In Malawi, over 60% of patients reported not being treated with respect by healthcare workers or clinic staff. It is reasonable to assume that feeling disrespected discourages return visits, and this may be especially true for women and vulnerable groups who already face social barriers to seeking care.



Heatmap of the percentage of public-clinic patients in 10 countries who experienced long wait times, unavailable medicines, disrespect, paying a bribe, and poor facilities.

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
section: Where You Live Within a Country Could Shape Your Access to Care
text:
Where You Live Within a Country Could Shape Your Access to Care
Whether roads are passable determines whether a clinic within walking distance is truly accessible. The interactive map allows readers to explore road quality by country (by hovering on a country) and while the relationship between road conditions and difficulty accessing care is not uniform, countries at the harder end of the access spectrum like Zimbabwe, have relatively lower average road quality scores.
Filtering by rural and urban area does not reveal any clear patterns either. In some countries urban residents report greater difficulty accessing care than rural ones (eg. Zimbabwe); in others the reverse is true (eg. Sudan).



Choropleth map of Africa showing the percentage of patients who found it difficult to access medical care, by country, with a settlement-type filter (static screenshot of the interactive Tableau map).

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
text:
The Missing Piece
What the data does suggest is that healthcare access in Africa is not easily generalisable. Distance alone is not the biggest constraint. Where you live matters, but patient experiences, availability of medicines, corruption and poor roads all build on each other in ways that a single indicator cannot and does not capture. So until facility capacity, quality of care and supporting infrastructure move forward together, access in theory and the care received in practice will remain two very different things.

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
text:
Data and tools

Data: Afrobarometer Round 9 (2021-23)
Tools: R for the static charts; Tableau for the interactive map

title: Bribes and Broken Roads May Be Bigger Barriers to Healthcare Than Distance Alone
text:
Chart design notes
Heatmap (what patients experience at a public clinic). This visualization is intended for a general audience of readers, policymakers, and global health advocates. It uses a waffle-style heat tile map to show self-reported negative experiences in public health facilities across selected countries, based on Afrobarometer Round 9 data. Countries are listed alongside key issues such as long wait times, unofficial payments, and medicine shortages, with each tile representing the share of respondents reporting each experience. Darker shades indicate higher prevalence, allowing quick comparison across countries and types of service failures, highlighting differences in quality of care that patients experience.
Dumbbell chart (clinic nearby versus care received). This visualization is intended for a general audience of readers, policymakers, and global health advocates. It uses a dumbbell plot to compare the proportion of communities with a health clinic within walking distance against the share of households reporting they received needed medical care across selected African countries. The purpose of this visualization is to challenge the assumption that geographic access to clinics alone is sufficient for people to receive care when they need it. It highlights that improving health outcomes requires not just building facilities closer to people, but ensuring that those facilities are usable, trusted, and able to meet demand.
Interactive map (difficulty accessing care). This visualization is intended for a general audience of readers, policymakers, and global health advocates. It uses an interactive map to show the share of people reporting difficulty accessing healthcare after visiting a public clinic, alongside average road quality by country. The map highlights how infrastructure shapes access to care. Countries with poorer road conditions, such as Zimbabwe, tend to report higher difficulty accessing services, though the relationship is not consistent across all contexts. Differences between rural and urban areas also vary widely, with no uniform pattern across countries. The purpose of this visualization is to show that access to healthcare depends not only on distance to facilities, but also on the quality of infrastructure.
Source for all three: Afrobarometer Round 9 Survey Data, afrobarometer.org/surveys-and-datasets/round-9-data

title: Rising BCG Coverage in Bangladesh Coincided with a Sharp Decline in Child Mortality
text: Connected scatterplot of BCG vaccination rate (%) against under-5 mortality rate per 1,000 for Bangladesh, 1981-2024, with an 85% coverage threshold marked.

title: Rising BCG Coverage in Bangladesh Coincided with a Sharp Decline in Child Mortality
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization is intended for public health policymakers and global health advocates, and is designed to be accessible to audiences with limited technical knowledge. The scatterplot, connected by a line, highlights Bangladesh’s trajectory from 1981 to 2024, showing the relationship between BCG vaccination coverage and under-5 mortality rates over time. The chart indicates that as vaccination rates rose from close to zero to above 85%, child mortality fell dramatically, from over 200 deaths per 1,000 to roughly 20. However, the steepest decline occurs after Bangladesh crosses the 85% vaccine coverage threshold. The intended takeaway is that improving vaccine coverage, particularly past critical thresholds, is one of the most effective levers available for reducing child mortality.

title: Rising BCG Coverage in Bangladesh Coincided with a Sharp Decline in Child Mortality
text:
Sources

UNICEF Child Health and Immunization Database: data.unicef.org/topic/child-health/immunization
www.childmortality.org

title: Electricity and Clean Cooking Access Are Both Far From Universal in Sub-Saharan Africa
text: Diverging bar chart of the percentage of population with access to clean cooking fuels and to electricity, urban versus rural, by world region.

title: Electricity and Clean Cooking Access Are Both Far From Universal in Sub-Saharan Africa
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization is intended for policymakers, development practitioners, and anyone interested in global energy access. It compares access to electricity and clean cooking fuels across regions, and is further broken down by urban and rural populations. The goal is to show how access differs not just across regions, but also between electricity and clean cooking and to highlight gaps in household energy access. So while electricity access is almost identical between rural and urban areas for most world regions, clean cooking access remains significantly lower and depends on urbanisation levels. Sub-Saharan Africa specifically sees a stark divide in rural vs urban and also access to electricity vs clean cooking fuel when compared to the rest of the world.

title: Electricity and Clean Cooking Access Are Both Far From Universal in Sub-Saharan Africa
text:
Sources

World Bank, World Development Indicators, SE4ALL: data360.worldbank.org/en/dataset/WB_SE4ALL

title: Women’s Bank Account Ownership Has Risen Globally But Unevenly (2011-2024)
text: Boxplots of the percentage of women with a bank account by World Bank region, 2011 versus 2024.

title: Women’s Bank Account Ownership Has Risen Globally But Unevenly (2011-2024)
text:
Purpose & audience
This visualization presents female bank account ownership rates across World Bank regions in 2011 and 2024. The intended audience is policymakers and development researchers (not the layperson) interested in the topic of women’s financial inclusion. The purpose is to support the point that while account ownership has expanded globally over the past thirteen years, progress has been largely uneven across geographical regions. Some regions like South and East Asia recorded dramatic gains in the median while some like the Middle East and North Africa have barely moved. The audience should be able to compare both the level and spread of ownership rates within regions, and point out the regions in which distributions have shifted versus remained flat.

title: Women’s Bank Account Ownership Has Risen Globally But Unevenly (2011-2024)
text:
Sources

Global Findex Database (World Bank)
